title: Four dangers for a swimmer
hook: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks: the dangers for someone new to the path

segments.voice: Yesterday: latukika. A rotten vine holds the quail only because it never pulls. Your line was it's only a creeper. Did you pull once? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

About five hundred monks arrive at a village called Cātumā with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, some of them newly ordained, and they're loud. Greeting the resident monks, finding beds, arranging bowls and robes, all at once. The Buddha hears the noise, asks what it is, and sends them all away. The local people and, the sutta says, a god named Brahmā Sahampati plead for them: they're new, they're like young seedlings that need water. The Buddha relents. And then, with the new ones sitting in front of him, he tells them what tends to drown beginners.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED MONKS, AND NOISE.` → `SENT AWAY.` → `LIKE SEEDLINGS THAT NEED WATER.`

segments.voice: Someone wading into a river, the sutta says, can expect four dangers: waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks. The Buddha names each one for a person who has just entered the training. The waves are anger and frustration at being taught. Do this, don't do that, look ahead, look behind, wear your robe this way. Someone who was used to giving instructions at home now has to take them from people younger than they are, and it stings. A person like this, the sutta says, can give up the training right there. The crocodiles are the stomach. Eat this, don't eat that, not now. The whirlpools are the five kinds of sensual pleasure: what's lovely to see, hear, smell, taste and touch, swirling around a new monk when he walks into the village. The fourth, the sharks, is sexual desire. The text, spoken to monks, names it through women; read today, it's the pull of attraction for anyone in training who has vowed celibacy. None of the four is deep philosophy. In the sutta, what sends a beginner home is being corrected. It's food. It's the scroll of things to want. It's attraction. Knowing which water you're in doesn't make the crocodile go away. But a swimmer who knows the river is less likely to be surprised. And a beginner who's been told the waves will come might feel them and think, ah, this is the wave they meant, instead of, this proves I don't belong here.
screen: `WAVES: ANGER AT BEING TAUGHT.` · `CROCODILES: THE STOMACH.` · `WHIRLPOOLS: THE FIVE PLEASURES.` · `SHARKS: SEXUAL DESIRE.` · then, large: `KNOW THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your four dangers. Sit and settle. Think of something you've started recently and want to keep: a practice, a job, a way of living. Ask, gently: what are my waves, the corrections that sting? My crocodile, the appetite? My whirlpool, the thing that pulls me off? My shark? Give each one a short name, silently. Then let the names go and rest with the breath, like floating. The bell holds the time.
Catuma. Waves, crocodiles, whirlpools and sharks: anger at being taught, the stomach, the five pleasures, and desire. Today's word.
Your line: know the water. Today, when one of your four shows up, name it: a wave, a crocodile, a whirlpool. Name it, and keep swimming. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Some monastic teachers use this sutta with new monks and nuns, so that the frustration of being corrected or the pull of food and pleasure can be recognized as a stage of training, not a reason to leave.

fork.setup: you're new to a practice, and someone younger corrects how you sit. you feel a flash of anger. in this sutta's picture, what is it?
fork.reveal: the waves are anger at being taught. the sutta names them so a beginner can recognize them, not drown in them.

trapdoor: what you thought: four dangers in a river.
what it means: anger at being taught, appetite, the five sensual pleasures and sexual desire: the four things the sutta says can turn a beginner back.
what a scholar hears: MN 67, the Cātumā Sutta, also includes the Buddha's test of Sāriputta and Moggallāna over who should look after the community once he sent the monks away.
recall: a lion's roar: a bold claim

notes: MN 67 paraphrased. The fourth danger (susukā, often 'sharks' or 'fierce fish') is explained in the text as women, addressed to celibate monks; the script says so plainly and then generalizes to sexual desire. A Keeper may prefer different wording.
The Sakyans of Cātumā and Brahmā Sahampati both intercede in the sutta (similes of seedlings without water and a calf without its mother); the script uses the seedling image only.
No original-language word given; 'ūmi' (wave) and 'susukā' could be added if a Keeper confirms spellings.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the five hundred monks were not all new (MN 67 says some were newly gone forth); removed 'Many turn back', 'rarely the deep philosophy', 'most often' and 'half of staying afloat' (unsourced claims); dropped the 'Picture' opener in the teach and a stock line; softened howItsDone.
